title: A Power Cut at Every Step: Two Slots and a Commit, and Why Overwriting the Running Release Bricks the Robot

questions.question: Why does copying the new release over the running one brick the robot when the power fails?
options: The copy is too slow to finish before the battery runs out
For the time it takes the slot is half old and half new, with the old hash, and there is no other slot to boot
The new files are signed and the old ones are not
Flash wears out when it is written in place
questions.explanation: Any cut after the first chunk and before the hash leaves a slot that is neither release, and nothing else to boot. 8 of the 10 possible cuts bricked the robot.

questions.question: In the two slot install, what is the last step and why last?
options: The move of the boot pointer: nothing before it changes what boots, and it is one write
Writing the hash and version: that is what makes the slot valid
Writing the last chunk: until then the release is incomplete
The reboot: nothing takes effect until then
questions.explanation: The chunks and the hash go into the slot that is not running. Only the pointer decides what boots, so it is moved last, in a single write.

questions.question: After the ninth of ten steps, which release does the robot boot?
options: Release 2: it is complete and valid
Neither: the install was interrupted
Release 1: release 2 is complete and valid in the other slot but the pointer has not moved
Whichever slot has the newer version
questions.explanation: The pointer still names slot 0. The new release sits finished in slot 1 and the old one has not been touched.

questions.question: Why can a cut install simply be run again?
options: It keeps a record of the step it reached and resumes there
The plan is made from what boots now and not from where the last attempt stopped
It locks the disk so that a second attempt waits
A cut install leaves both slots valid by luck
questions.explanation: It needs no memory of the failure. An installer that must work out where it stopped has a second thing to get wrong. Starting from what boots now, 11 of 11 cut installs finished on release 2.

questions.question: A chunk of the new release is damaged after the switch. What boots?
options: Release 2, with the damaged chunk skipped
Nothing: the pointer names an invalid slot
Release 2, after the chunk is repaired from slot 0
The release before, from the other slot: the slot is invalid and the fallback is the design
questions.explanation: The boot checks the slot's hash and, finding it wrong, takes the other slot. The previous release is always there because the slots alternate.

questions.question: What does this scheme assume about the hardware that you must test on the real robot?
options: That the disk has two physical drives
That flash never wears out
That a single write is atomic
That the boot loader can be updated too
questions.explanation: A power cut falls between steps and never inside one: pull the real power hundreds of times. The argument rests on a power cut never landing in the middle of a write. Whether that holds for this flash is found by pulling the power, many times.
